paragraphs: Contextual bandit algorithms choose actions using information about the current situation and learn from the rewards they receive. Reward prediction makes these algorithms flexible, but it can also create a vulnerability: the chosen model may not accurately represent the true rewards. This paper asks how an algorithm can retain computational efficiency while its performance deteriorates gracefully as that modeling mismatch grows.

The authors introduce algorithms that adapt to an unknown amount of misspecification, covering both finite and infinite action spaces. Their approach assumes access to an online square-loss regression oracle: a component that learns reward predictions through squared prediction error. The bandit algorithm uses this component without needing the misspecification level in advance.

The paper establishes optimal regret guarantees, including optimal dependence on the modeling error. For linear models with infinitely many actions, its bound combines a term growing with the square root of the interaction horizon and a misspecification term growing linearly. The result explains how approximation error affects achievable performance while showing that prior knowledge of that error is unnecessary for the stated guarantee.
neurips-2020-adapting-to-misspecificatio.tldr: New contextual bandit algorithms achieve optimal regret while adapting to an unknown degree of reward-model misspecification.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness concerns whether small changes to an input can alter a classifier’s prediction. This paper studies certified robustness, where a mathematical guarantee establishes protection against a specified class of perturbations. Its central idea is to exploit low-rank representations that occur naturally in data such as images, using their structure to strengthen the guarantees available for neural networks.

For perturbations measured by the L2 norm, the authors use these representations to improve on randomized smoothing guarantees on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. They also investigate L-infinity perturbations, which constrain the largest individual input change. Experiments indicate that natural low-rank representations possess robustness properties that support substantially stronger certificates in this setting.

Connecting these two types of guarantees requires bounding how the representation transforms perturbations. The authors express that connection through an infinity-to-two matrix operator norm and develop a fast algorithm that supplies provable upper bounds on it. This algorithm uses multiplicative weight updates and improves existing algorithmic guarantees for the norm-bounding problem, making the certification machinery a contribution alongside the representation-based robustness results.
neurips-2020-adversarial-robustness-via-.tldr: Natural low-rank representations strengthen adversarial robustness certificates, supported by a new algorithm for bounding how representations transform perturbations.

paragraphs: A prediction problem can have several plausible outputs for the same input. In that situation, predicting the conditional average can obscure the distinct outcomes that the data actually favors. Modal regression instead seeks the peaks of the conditional output distribution. The paper develops a parametric approach to this problem, motivated by the scaling difficulties of many existing nonparametric methods.

The method learns a joint function of inputs and candidate outputs. Its training objective is developed using the implicit function theorem, allowing the model to represent relationships with multiple output values. This formulation also makes it possible to use parametric approximators such as neural networks to capture complex relationships between the inputs and targets.

On synthetic problems, the authors show that the approach can recover conditional modes, learn multivalued functions, and handle high-dimensional inputs effectively. It can also outperform alternatives on certain single-mode problems, particularly those involving high-frequency functions. Results on a real-world modal regression task and two ordinary regression datasets are competitive, suggesting that the formulation has uses beyond explicitly multimodal prediction.
neurips-2020-an-implicit-function-learni.tldr: An implicit-function-based regression objective learns conditional modes, enabling parametric models to represent multiple plausible outputs for one input.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means using familiar parts in combinations that were not previously encountered. The paper addresses the difficulty neural models have with this capability. Its starting point is a cognitive account in which symbolic functions operate on variable slots: reusable structures can accept different contents, allowing known operations and components to participate in new combinations.

The authors connect that idea to a neural model with memory and analytical expressions. Two cooperating modules, called Composer and Solver, form the architecture. Together, they provide a way to organize learning around compositional structure while remaining trainable as one system. A hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm supplies the end-to-end training procedure.

Experiments use the SCAN benchmark to assess whether the model can generalize compositionally. The authors report 100% accuracy on all the challenges addressed by previous work in that benchmark. This is strong evidence for the proposed architecture within the reported evaluation. The contribution is a concrete connection between symbolic compositional ideas and trainable neural machinery, with benchmark results showing that this connection can support successful recombination.
neurips-2020-compositional-generalizatio.tldr: A memory-augmented Composer–Solver model learns analytical expressions and achieves 100% accuracy on the reported SCAN compositional generalization challenges.

paragraphs: Detecting a change in a sequence and establishing that the detected change is statistically reliable are separate problems. A detection algorithm deliberately selects locations that look unusual, so evaluating those locations must account for that selection. This paper develops significance testing for changepoints chosen by an optimal detection algorithm based on dynamic programming.

The method uses selective inference to compute valid p-values for the selected changepoints. These guarantees are exact rather than dependent on a large-sample approximation. A central challenge is that selective inference can lose statistical power when it conditions on too much information about how the result was selected. The authors introduce parametric dynamic programming to conduct the inference with minimal conditioning.

Reducing unnecessary conditioning allows the procedure to retain greater ability to identify significant changes while accounting for selection. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets provide evidence of higher statistical power than existing methods, along with reasonable computational efficiency and useful practical results. The contribution therefore links optimal changepoint detection to a more informative assessment of whether its discoveries are statistically meaningful.
neurips-2020-computing-valid-p-value-for.tldr: Parametric dynamic programming enables exact selective p-values for detected changepoints while reducing the conditioning that can weaken statistical power.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to train a model so that it can adapt to individual tasks. MAML performs this adaptation by updating all model parameters, which can make both task adaptation and training the shared initialization computationally expensive. ANIL reduces that expense by adapting only a small parameter subset. This paper supplies a theoretical analysis of ANIL’s convergence and computational complexity.

The analysis separates two cases according to the shape of the task-specific inner-loop loss: strongly convex and nonconvex. That distinction changes how additional adaptation steps affect overall convergence. For a strongly convex inner-loop loss, increasing the number of gradient steps improves the convergence rate. For a nonconvex loss, increasing that number produces a slower rate in the authors’ analysis.

These results show why the amount of task-specific adaptation cannot be assessed independently of the optimization geometry. The complexity analysis also quantifies ANIL’s efficiency advantage over MAML, providing theoretical support for its computational appeal. Experiments on standard few-shot learning benchmarks support the theoretical findings, connecting the convergence analysis to the behavior observed in meta-learning tasks.
neurips-2020-convergence-of-meta-learnin.tldr: ANIL’s convergence depends on inner-loop loss geometry, with more adaptation steps helping the strongly convex case but slowing the analyzed nonconvex case.

paragraphs: Deep networks can fit incorrect labels as well as meaningful patterns, making noisy training data a source of overfitting. This paper addresses that problem through the choice of training examples. It proposes selecting weighted subsets, called coresets, of clean data points and connects the structure of those subsets to theoretical guarantees for robust neural-network training.

The selection aims to produce an approximately low-rank Jacobian matrix, which describes how model outputs change as parameters change. Thus, the method considers the structure of the training problem induced by the selected examples, beyond simply reducing the number of examples. The authors prove that gradient descent applied to the proposed subsets does not overfit the noisy labels.

Extensive experiments support the theory and report substantially better performance than existing methods. The abstract gives an accuracy increase of 6% on CIFAR-10 with 80% noisy labels and 7% on mini Webvision. These findings connect a specific mathematical property of weighted training subsets with practical resistance to label noise, showing how data selection can become part of the robustness mechanism.
neurips-2020-coresets-for-robust-trainin.tldr: Weighted coresets with approximately low-rank Jacobians support theoretical protection against fitting noisy labels and improve accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Predicting how a visual-cortex neuron responds to stimuli usually requires fitting a model to that neuron. Repeating this optimization for newly observed neurons takes time and can obstruct real-time experiments. This paper reframes the task as K-shot prediction: infer a neuron’s response properties directly from a small collection of stimulus–response observations.

The authors develop a Factorized Neural Process that converts those observations into a latent representation with two parts. One represents receptive-field location, and the other represents properties of the neuron’s tuning function. The representation is inferred in a single forward pass through the network, avoiding the time-consuming parameter optimization otherwise needed to model each newly observed neuron.

On simulated responses, predictions and reconstructed receptive fields approach the true values as more trials become available. On real visual-cortex data, predictive accuracy is comparable to optimization-based methods and better when K is small, while inference is substantially faster. These findings support the authors’ expectation that rapid response modeling could make neural-network models easier to integrate into real-time neuroscience experiments.
neurips-2020-factorized-neural-processes.tldr: A Factorized Neural Process predicts a neuron’s responses from a few observations in one forward pass, matching or exceeding optimization-based accuracy in reported settings.

paragraphs: Structured prediction can involve assigning labels to graph nodes using noisy evidence about individual nodes and their connections. Previous results showed that certain well-connected graphs permit recovery of every true binary label with high probability and in polynomial time. This paper asks how that recovery problem changes when the true labeling satisfies a statistical-parity fairness condition.

The analysis considers a particular generative model on an undirected connected graph, with one noisy observation per node and edge. Within this setting, adding the fairness constraint improves the probability of recovering the complete true assignment. The result demonstrates a case where a known fairness property supplies useful information for inference, rather than merely introducing a competing prediction requirement.

The authors explain this improvement theoretically and provide experiments showing exact recovery on graphs with weak expansion, including grids. The scope matters: the result concerns recovering an already fair assignment under the studied model. As an additional mathematical contribution, the analysis yields a tighter lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue than one obtainable from Weyl’s inequality.
neurips-2020-fairness-constraints-can-he.tldr: Under a studied graph-based generative model, a statistical-parity constraint improves the probability of exactly recovering a fair binary labeling.

paragraphs: Sparse adversarial attacks try to fool an image classifier by changing only a few pixels. Their effectiveness depends on both how many pixels they alter and how noticeable those alterations become. GreedyFool addresses these two concerns together, seeking changes that strongly affect the model while taking visual distortion into account during the selection process.

The method has two stages. First, it greedily selects promising pixel locations using both a gradient signal, which guides the attack, and a distortion map, which guides invisibility. It then enters a reduction stage that removes less important selected points. This second stage trims the set of modifications after the initial attack construction.

Experiments report that GreedyFool needs about one-third as many modified pixels as the compared state-of-the-art method under the same sparse perturbation setting. For targeted attacks, it reports a 9.96% higher success rate under an equal pixel budget. These findings show an empirical benefit from combining attack effectiveness and distortion awareness, then explicitly revisiting whether every chosen modification remains necessary.
neurips-2020-greedyfool-distortion-aware.tldr: GreedyFool combines gradient and distortion information with a pruning stage to produce successful adversarial attacks using fewer modified pixels.

paragraphs: An agent exploring without a reward function still needs a useful learning objective. This paper asks it to learn near-optimal policies for reaching every state that is incrementally reachable within an expected step budget from a reference state. The resulting knowledge describes where the agent can go and how to get there before a particular reward-driven task is supplied.

The proposed algorithm, DisCo, alternates between discovering states and improving an estimated environment model. It uses that model to compute goal-conditioned policies for newly discovered destinations. Its sample-complexity bound improves the dependence on the step budget and accuracy requirement relative to the earlier incremental exploration algorithm, while adding a factor for the dynamics’ branching structure.

That tradeoff is favorable when the branching factor is small, as the authors say it is in many environments of interest. DisCo also supports cost-sensitive shortest-path tasks on the reachable states, with a policy optimality guarantee that depends on the minimum cost. Preliminary experiments support the theoretical findings, linking reward-free exploration to reusable knowledge for later navigation objectives.
neurips-2020-improved-sample-complexity-.tldr: DisCo learns reusable goal-reaching policies without rewards, improving exploration bounds while introducing a dependence on the environment’s branching factor.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can excel on familiar levels yet perform poorly on new ones that share the same underlying dynamics. This paper studies that gap through partially observable decision processes, treating training levels as instances. It proves that repeatedly using instances changes the effective Markov dynamics experienced during training, independently of the agent’s exploration strategy.

This change affects what the agent learns to remember and exploit. Maximizing training rewards can favor instance-specific speed-running behavior over policies that generalize, because the more general policies can be worse on the training set. The authors derive bounds connecting the training–test value gap to the number of training instances, giving a theoretical account of this pressure toward specialization.

Their proposed remedy trains a shared belief representation across an ensemble of specialized policies. A consensus policy derived from the ensemble collects data, preventing instance-specific exploitation in that collection process. Experiments on CoinRun support the analysis and the proposed solution. The work ties generalization failures to the interaction between reused environments, learned beliefs, and the policy responsible for gathering experience.
neurips-2020-instance-based-generalizati.tldr: Reusing training levels can encourage instance-specific policies; shared belief learning and consensus-based data collection improve generalization in CoinRun experiments.

paragraphs: JAX MD is a software framework for differentiable physics, with molecular dynamics as its main focus. Its defining feature is that a simulation is itself a differentiable function. This lets users compute derivatives through an entire simulated trajectory and use them for meta-optimization, connecting the behavior produced by a simulation to an optimization process.

The package includes statistical-physics simulation environments, interaction potentials, and neural networks designed to fit into those environments without additional integration code. Its underlying operations include spatial partitioning, and the authors report that these building blocks support simulations with hundreds of thousands of particles on a single GPU. The same primitives are flexible enough to support workloads beyond molecular dynamics.

Examples demonstrate graph neural networks embedded in traditional simulations, meta-optimization through particle-packing minimization, and a simulation of multiple flocking agents. These examples illustrate both the integration of learned components with physical simulation and the wider usefulness of the computational infrastructure. The contribution is a reusable framework that brings differentiability, simulation components, and scaling operations together.
neurips-2020-jax-md-a-framework-for-diff.tldr: JAX MD combines scalable physics simulation with differentiable trajectories and integrated neural components to support simulation-based meta-optimization.

paragraphs: Decision trees and random forests are strong predictors, but their usual discriminative formulation does not provide a principled account of missing inputs or unusual observations. This paper connects these models to probabilistic circuits, allowing them to be interpreted as generative models. The resulting Generative Decision Trees and Generative Forests retain familiar tree-model characteristics while representing a joint distribution over features.

Having that distribution changes how incomplete inputs can be processed. The models can marginalize missing features, accounting for their possible values through the probability model. The authors also establish consistency across any pattern of missing input features when the data is missing at random, subject to assumptions commonly used in Bayes-consistency results.

Experiments show that these models often outperform common missing-data treatments, including K-nearest-neighbor imputation. Their probabilistic interpretation also provides an outlier signal through the marginal probability assigned to observed features. The contribution therefore extends familiar prediction tools with a unified mechanism for incomplete and atypical inputs, while preserving explicit conditions on the theoretical missing-data guarantee.
neurips-2020-joints-in-random-forests-e6.tldr: A probabilistic-circuit interpretation turns trees and forests into joint-distribution models that can marginalize missing features and detect outliers.

paragraphs: Total variation regularization encourages a recovered signal to consist of relatively constant segments separated by changes. It does this by penalizing the size of first-order differences through an L1 constraint. Solving the resulting optimization problem with standard iterative methods can require many steps. This paper explores learning solver parameters to accelerate the process for one-dimensional signals.

The authors unfold proximal gradient descent into a trainable sequence of operations. They examine two formulations of the underlying problem and find that using the synthesis formulation leads to slower performance. The analysis formulation presents a different obstacle: training requires derivatives through the proximal operator, the operation that handles the regularization within each iteration.

The main contribution is the development and characterization of two ways to compute those derivatives. The authors describe their respective benefits and limitations and identify the regime where the learned approach can improve on iterative procedures. Experiments on synthetic and real data support those findings. The work makes differentiating through the solver a central part of understanding when learned acceleration is useful.
neurips-2020-learning-to-solve-tv-regula.tldr: Two approaches to differentiating through the total-variation proximal operator enable learned acceleration of one-dimensional solvers in the studied regimes.

paragraphs: Regularization can improve generalization across many kinds of models, while transfer learning draws useful knowledge from previously available data. This paper seeks to combine those strengths through a learned perturbation function called MetaPerturb. The goal is to transfer a regularizing behavior across tasks and architectures, including settings that differ from the source used to learn it.

MetaPerturb is implemented as a lightweight set-based network shared across layers. Its behavior does not depend on input order or input size, helping it accommodate different architectures. A meta-learning framework trains the perturbation function jointly across heterogeneous tasks in parallel, exposing it to varied distributions across both layers and tasks.

The authors evaluate a perturbation learned on a particular source domain and architecture by applying it during training on diverse target datasets and neural architectures. Models trained with MetaPerturb significantly outperform the compared regularizers and fine-tuning baselines on most evaluated tasks and architectures. The reported gains come with negligible additional parameter size and no hyperparameters to tune, supporting the usefulness of transferring a learned training regularizer.
neurips-2020-metaperturb-transferable-re.tldr: MetaPerturb learns a lightweight perturbation regularizer that transfers across heterogeneous tasks and architectures, improving most reported evaluations with negligible parameter overhead.

paragraphs: Reward decomposition breaks an overall reinforcement learning reward into smaller components, an approach that can improve sample efficiency. Discovering useful components is difficult when the decomposition depends strongly on the current policy. Such dependence can constrain how differently the policies associated with separate sub-rewards behave. This paper approaches the problem through the state features each reward component needs.

The authors propose principles of compactness and uniqueness. Each sub-reward should rely on a small set of relevant features while retaining something distinctive from the other sub-rewards. These principles guide a deep learning algorithm, RD², that learns the reward decomposition and the corresponding representation decomposition together. The representation is therefore part of what defines the separation between reward components.

Evaluation includes a toy problem with a known true reward structure and Atari environments whose reward structure is unknown to the agent. The reported results demonstrate effectiveness against existing reward-decomposition methods. The central contribution is a feature-based criterion for discovering reward components, connecting the meaning of each component to the information needed to represent it.
neurips-2020-rd-2-reward-decomposition-w.tldr: RD² jointly decomposes rewards and representations, encouraging each sub-reward to depend on a compact and distinctive set of features.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis works backward from a desired molecule toward building blocks that could be used to make it. Automated predictions can assist this planning, but the authors identify cumbersome methods and unclear prediction rationales as problems with existing approaches. RetroXpert addresses these concerns by separating retrosynthetic expansion into two chemically motivated steps within a template-free method.

First, a graph neural network identifies a potential reaction center in the target molecule and generates intermediate synthons. These intermediates express a proposed decomposition of the target. Second, a reactant-generation model predicts the reactants associated with those synthons. This staged design makes the proposed decomposition an explicit intermediate result connecting the target molecule to the generated reactants.

The authors report that RetroXpert outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin and provides chemically reasonable interpretations. The interpretability comes from exposing meaningful stages of the prediction process: where a reaction might occur and which reactants correspond to the resulting intermediates. The reported findings support this decomposition as a useful structure for automatic retrosynthetic expansion.
neurips-2020-retroxpert-decompose-retros.tldr: RetroXpert predicts reaction centers and intermediate synthons before generating reactants, improving reported retrosynthesis performance while exposing chemically meaningful intermediate decisions.

paragraphs: Design problems can require searching through complicated structured objects while each quality evaluation is expensive. A deep generative model offers a lower-dimensional, continuous space in which to conduct that search. This paper argues that the usefulness of this latent space should itself be maintained during optimization, because the search depends on the representation the model provides.

The method periodically retrains the generative model using points evaluated along the optimization trajectory. It weights those points according to their objective values, steering the learned representation toward the optimization objective. The search and representation learning therefore interact: evaluations provide information for improving the latent space, which then supports subsequent optimization.

The authors present weighted retraining as an addition that can be implemented readily on top of existing methods. Experiments on synthetic and real-world optimization problems show significant gains in efficiency and performance. These results support actively adapting the generative model as evaluations accumulate, particularly in the expensive black-box setting where making productive use of each queried point is a central concern.
neurips-2020-sample-efficient-optimizati.tldr: Periodically retraining a generative model with objective-weighted observations makes its latent space more useful for sample-efficient black-box optimization.

paragraphs: Learning to reconstruct a three-dimensional object from an image often requires expensive training annotations. Even methods that avoid ground-truth 3D shapes can require several annotated views of each object. SDF-SRN addresses this training-data requirement by learning from only one view per object, using two-dimensional silhouette supervision to support three-dimensional shape reconstruction.

The method represents shapes implicitly through signed distance functions. This representation allows it to handle arbitrary shape topologies present in the data. To learn the representation from silhouettes, the authors derive a differentiable rendering formulation. That formulation connects the predicted three-dimensional shape to the two-dimensional supervision available during training.

The authors report better performance than the state of the art under challenging single-view supervision conditions on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The significance is the combination of a flexible shape representation and a reduced annotation requirement. Training can use a single annotated view of an object rather than requiring multiple views of that same instance, making the approach more useful for the real-world scenarios motivating the work.
neurips-2020-sdf-srn-learning-signed-dis.tldr: SDF-SRN learns implicit 3D shapes from single-view silhouette supervision through a new differentiable rendering formulation.

paragraphs: Domain-adaptive object re-identification transfers knowledge from labeled source images to an unlabeled target domain. Pseudo-labeling can help, but imperfect clustering and differences between domains leave useful information underused. This paper proposes a contrastive learning framework that brings several forms of supervision into a shared training process, including target examples that have not been assigned to clusters.

Its hybrid memory supplies source-class, target-cluster, and individual unclustered-target signals. The model learns to distinguish all three kinds jointly. A self-paced procedure gradually produces more reliable target clusters, updating both the memory and the learning targets. The authors identify this progressive refinement as a key contributor to the method’s performance.

The method outperforms existing approaches on multiple domain-adaptation tasks and also improves source-domain performance without extra annotations. A generalized version for unsupervised re-identification reports improvements of 16.7% on Market-1501 and 7.9% on MSMT17 over state-of-the-art algorithms. These findings support using both grouped and ungrouped target information while improving the reliability of the groups throughout learning.
neurips-2020-self-paced-contrastive-lear.tldr: Hybrid memory combines labeled source classes, target clusters, and unclustered instances while self-paced refinement improves domain-adaptive re-identification.

paragraphs: Regression trees organize prediction around regions of the input space. This paper generalizes that structure into Probabilistic Regression trees, aiming to adapt to the smoothness of the relationship between inputs and outputs while preserving interpretability and robustness to noise. The key change is how an observation participates in the regions defined by a tree.

Each observation is associated with all regions through a probability distribution that reflects its distance from them. This probabilistic association provides a way to express smoother predictive relationships within a tree-based model. The authors establish consistency: the relevant prediction error tends to zero as the sample size grows without bound. They note that comparable results had not been established for earlier soft-tree and smooth-transition proposals.

The paper also explains how to use these trees within random forests and gradient-boosted trees, extending the construction to familiar ensemble methods. Extensive experiments illustrate benefits in prediction performance, interpretability, and noise robustness. Together, the results connect a smoother region-assignment mechanism with both an asymptotic guarantee and empirical evidence of practical usefulness.
neurips-2020-smooth-and-consistent-proba.tldr: Probabilistic Regression trees associate observations with multiple regions to support smooth predictions, consistency guarantees, and robust tree ensembles.

paragraphs: Adapting a model on an edge device requires fitting training into a small memory budget. TinyTL focuses on intermediate activations, which the authors identify as the main memory bottleneck. Simply reducing the number of trainable parameters does not directly resolve that cost. The method instead freezes model weights and trains bias modules, avoiding the associated need to retain intermediate activations.

To preserve adaptation capacity, TinyTL adds a lite residual module that learns small residual feature maps to refine the feature extractor. The reported memory overhead for this module is 3.8%. This gives the model a way to adjust its features while retaining the memory advantages of the restricted training scheme.

Experiments report up to 6.5-fold memory savings with little accuracy loss relative to full-network fine-tuning. Compared with last-layer fine-tuning, accuracy improves by up to 34.1% with little memory overhead. Combined with feature-extractor adaptation, the method achieves 7.3–12.9-fold memory savings without sacrificing accuracy relative to full Inception-V3 fine-tuning. These results show the practical value of targeting activation storage.
neurips-2020-tinytl-reduce-memory-not-pa.tldr: TinyTL reduces on-device training memory by freezing weights and learning compact bias and residual modules that preserve useful adaptation capacity.

paragraphs: Real-world datasets often mix categorical, ordered, and continuous features. Even features of the same type can have very different individual distributions. These differences can make deep generative modeling difficult. VAEM extends the variational autoencoder to address both sources of heterogeneity, with the aim of making generative modeling useful across a broader range of data.

The model is trained in two stages. The first stage gives the second a more uniform representation of the original features, reducing the difficulties caused by their differing types and distributions. This separates the work of accommodating heterogeneous inputs from the later modeling stage. The authors also extend the approach to data in which some values are unobserved.

Evaluation covers generating data, predicting missing values, and selecting features sequentially. These tasks test several ways a model of heterogeneous data can be used, including settings with incomplete information. The reported results support the authors’ claim that VAEM broadens the practical reach of deep generative models by making their training better suited to mixed and unevenly distributed features.
neurips-2020-vaem-a-deep-generative-mode.tldr: VAEM uses two-stage training to make heterogeneous features more uniform for generative modeling, including generation and prediction with missing data.

paragraphs: Neural-network pruning searches for smaller models by removing parameters from a larger network. The related lottery-ticket question asks whether small subnetworks can retain strong performance when trained with a comparable budget. This paper revisits how such subnetworks are found and proposes Continuous Sparsification, a method that makes sparsity part of an optimization objective.

The method uses a new approximation to L0 regularization, which targets the number of nonzero parameters but is otherwise intractable to optimize directly. The authors evaluate it for both pruning and ticket search. In their ticket-search evaluation, the objective is to identify sparse subnetworks that can be successfully retrained from an early training iterate.

Experiments report improvements over leading heuristic methods for both objectives across models and datasets, including VGG on CIFAR-10 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet. Continuous Sparsification also supports fast parallel ticket search. These findings provide empirical support for the proposed optimization-based sparsity mechanism and its usefulness in discovering retrainable subnetworks; they do not turn the broader Lottery Ticket Hypothesis into a universal theorem.
neurips-2020-winning-the-lottery-with-co.tldr: Continuous Sparsification approximates L0 regularization to improve neural-network pruning and the search for sparse subnetworks that can be retrained successfully.
